newsitem.title: NETHERLANDS: U.S. weather market leaves Europe feeds trade cold.
newsitem.headline: U.S. weather market leaves Europe feeds trade cold.

text.p: Unpredictable price swings on the CBOT soycomplex in the United States have killed off already depressed demand for meals and feeds in Europe, leaving traders handling only pockets of nearby business.
"We're living in a weather market and it has killed off business in Europe," said Arie van Dijk, analyst at market statisticians Stigevo.
Traders said forecasts of hot, dry weather had been replaced by showers, taking the shine off prices in Project A overnight trade and putting the market back on the defensive.
In the near term, Van Dijk said he expected a further cold front through the midwest, bringing a 75 percent chance of rain to soy crop areas. Temperatures would also fall this week.
"It seems the weather will not be giving us any worries this week and crop conditions look good, for the moment," he said.
But traders said a degree of unpredicatbility remained.
"Chicago should open lower this afternoon, but you never know. It makes people very uncertain," said one senior trader.
As a result, there were no trades reported in early Europe.
The strong dollar was another inhibiting factor, with traders saying that only a five to seven cent reduction in the mark rate would spark any business.

Flood-related damage in central Europe is not such a key market factor yet, but traders said they were keeping an eye on the situation. Poland is expected to have to import somewhere in the region of 450,000 tonnes of rapeseed due to a damaged crop.
Its rapeseed crop had already been cut by a severe winter and the recent floods have knocked another 100,000 tonnes off the expected size, traders said.
The havest is now seen around 350,000 tonnes and with a crushing capacity of 800,000 tonnes, imports were inevitable.
Van Dijk said he though Germany, expecting a bumper rapeseed crop this year, would be the preferred market for Polish buyers as Canadian canola was still too expensive.
He reckoned the country would also need to import around 200,000 tonnes of rapemeal.
But in general, the physical market was still plagued by slack demand.

Cattlefeed demand is seasonally depressed with cows grazing in fields, and pigfeed offtake in the Netherlands has been decimated by the swine fever epidemic. The two factors have combined to send some prices down to the bargain basement.
"Products such as citrusplup are historically low and in the next two months could fall even further," Van Dijk said.
The situation has been compounded by heavy arrivals into continental Europe from Brazil over the next quarter, he said.
"We could see prices recovering in the latter part of the year as consumers cover for the winter months, but not before."
